page: Amazon Web Services d3.4xlarge is a dense storage instance powered by the AWS Nitro hypervisor. It features an x86_64 Intel Xeon 8259CL processor with 16 vCPUs (8 physical cores with hyper-threading) running at 3.1 GHz. The instance is equipped with 128.0 GB of DDR4 memory operating at 3 GHz, providing 8.0 GB of RAM per core. It includes a massive 23,760 GB of local HDD storage, but lacks any GPU accelerators. Network connectivity is rated at a 12 Gbps baseline.

Performance benchmarks indicate a clear tradeoff between single-core and multi-core capabilities. Single-core performance is weak, as shown by stress-ng single-core and Geekbench single-core scores falling into the bottom 25%. However, multi-core performance and memory bandwidth scale to average levels (middle 50%), as demonstrated by the Passmark CPU score and multi-threaded Geekbench results. Cryptographic and vector operations are supported via AVX and AVX-512 instruction sets, though newer extensions like AVX-512 VNNI and AMX are absent.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the d3.4xlarge offers high storage density per resource unit, trading off high-speed SSD performance for massive HDD capacity. This makes it qualitatively cost-effective for workloads requiring large sequential data access rather than low-latency random I/O. Appropriate workloads include distributed file systems, data lakes, big data analytics, and large-scale log processing where massive local storage capacity is prioritized over raw single-threaded compute speed.
description: Amazon Web Services d3.4xlarge is a dense storage instance utilizing the AWS Nitro hypervisor and an x86_64 Intel Xeon 8259CL processor. It features 16 dedicated vCPUs (8 physical cores) running at 3.1 GHz, 128.0 GB of DDR4 RAM, and a massive 23,760 GB of local HDD storage, with a baseline network bandwidth of 12 Gbps. Benchmark data reveals a distinct performance profile: single-core CPU execution and single-threaded decompression are weak, placing in the bottom 25%, while multi-core performance, memory bandwidth, and database operations achieve average, middle-50% ratings. Lacking a GPU, this instance trades off high-speed random I/O and single-threaded compute for massive storage capacity and balanced multi-core throughput. It is suited for storage-heavy workloads, such as distributed file systems, data warehousing, and large-scale log processing.
